entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Iset (also Aset; a theophoric name related to Isis) was an ancient Egyptian royal woman of the Twentieth Dynasty who held the prestigious title God’s Wife of Amun, a pinnacle of female religious office at Thebes. God’s Wives of Amun controlled extensive temple estates, performed rituals as the earthly consort of the god Amun, and could wield political influence in Upper Egypt during the late New Kingdom, when royal power and Theban priesthood negotiated authority.

Though less famous than some earlier or later God’s Wives, Iset belongs to the institutional history that made Theban priestly–royal women central to late New Kingdom and Third Intermediate religious politics. Her office illustrates how Egyptian kingship sacralised elite women as mediators of Amun’s cult, tying dynastic legitimacy to Karnak’s wealth. Prosopographical and monumental evidence for Twentieth-Dynasty God’s Wives remains thinner than for the Twenty-Fifth–Twenty-Sixth Dynasty holders, but Iset is an important named link in that sequence.
